label: Guide for professionals
title: Becoming an autism assessor in the UK
metaTitle: How to become an autism assessor in the UK: tools, training and jobs | ND Resources
description: A UK guide to autism assessment for professionals: how NICE assessment pathways work for children and adults, the tools used (ADOS-2, ADI-R, DISCO and more), how assessors train, and how to find assessor jobs.
lede: How autism assessment works in the UK, the tools assessors use, how those skills are learnt, and how to find work as an assessor in the NHS or with private providers.
summary: In the UK, autism is diagnosed by registered clinicians (usually psychologists, psychiatrists or paediatricians), often working with speech and language therapists, occupational therapists and nurses in a multidisciplinary team.
Assessments follow NICE guidance: CG128 for children and young people, CG142 for adults. No single test or questionnaire can diagnose autism on its own.
The best-known tools are the ADOS-2 (an observation) and the ADI-R (a developmental interview). Clinical training in each takes 2 to 5 days and costs roughly £600 to £1,500 (November 2026).
Most assessors build experience in the NHS, then many also work for private or Right to Choose providers. Jobs are advertised on NHS Jobs, Trac, BPS Appointments and provider websites.

sections.heading: How autism assessment works in the UK
sections.html:
An autism assessment is a structured process that gathers information from several sources and then compares it with agreed diagnostic criteria. In the NHS in England, assessors are asked to describe autism using ICD-11 (the World Health Organization's classification), while the NHS still records diagnoses with ICD-10 codes. Many private services also refer to DSM-5-TR (the American classification). Both describe the same two areas: persistent differences in social communication and interaction, and restricted or repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or sensory experience, present from early development.

The national guidance

  • NICE CG128 covers children and young people under 19 in England and Wales.
  • NICE CG142 covers adults.
  • NHS England's national framework for all-age autism assessment pathways and its operational guidance (2023) tell local NHS services how to organise assessment.
  • Scotland follows SIGN 145. Wales and Northern Ireland have their own service models built on similar principles.

Who carries out the assessment

For children, NICE CG128 recommends a local multidisciplinary autism team whose core members are a paediatrician and/or child and adolescent psychiatrist, a speech and language therapist, and a psychologist experienced with autistic children. The team should also have access to occupational therapy and other specialists.

For adults, NICE CG142 says assessment should be done by professionals who are trained and competent, and should be team-based and draw on a range of professions where possible.

NHS England's framework adds a useful distinction. A standard assessment can be done by one or more suitably qualified clinicians. An enhanced assessment involves two or more clinicians and uses validated tools, a clinical interview and observation. It defines a clinician as someone registered with the GMC, HCPC or NMC, and is clear that registration alone does not make someone competent to assess autism: specific training is needed too. Paediatricians, psychiatrists and clinical psychologists can usually cover every part of an assessment; speech and language therapists and occupational therapists usually contribute as part of a team.

What a full assessment includes

  • Concerns and context: what the person, family or referrer has noticed, and life at home, school or work.
  • Developmental history: usually a structured interview with a parent or someone who knew the person as a child.
  • Observation and interaction: time spent with the person, often using a structured observation such as the ADOS-2.
  • Health history and, for children, a physical examination.
  • Differential diagnosis: thinking about what else could explain the picture, such as language disorder, learning disability, trauma, attachment difficulties, anxiety or ADHD.
  • Co-occurring conditions: checking for ADHD, anxiety, sleep problems, epilepsy and others.
  • A profile of strengths and needs, not only a yes or no answer.
  • Feedback and a written report, shared sensitively, with a follow-up offered. CG128 suggests a follow-up within 6 weeks for children.

NICE says a child's assessment should start within 3 months of referral to the autism team. In practice, waits are often far longer: NHS England reported more than 125,000 people waiting for an autism assessment in mental health services in 2022, and numbers have grown since.

The single most important principle: diagnosis is a clinical judgement made from all the information together. NICE is explicit that no autism-specific tool should be relied on alone to diagnose autism, and screening questionnaires should never be used to make or rule out a diagnosis.

sections.heading: Children and adults: what differs
sections.html:
Children and young people

  • Usually referred by a GP, health visitor, school or SENCO.
  • Parents' account of early development is central.
  • Information from nursery or school is usually requested.
  • Led by community paediatrics or CAMHS, depending on age and area.
  • Outcome feeds into school support and, where needed, an EHC needs assessment.

Adults

  • Often self-referred to a GP, who may use the AQ-10 screen. NICE CG142 suggests offering a full assessment when the score is above 6 or clinical judgement suggests autism.
  • Early history may be hard to get, so assessors rely more on the person's own account.
  • Many adults, especially women and people who mask, have learned to hide their differences, so observation alone can miss autism.
  • Mental health history matters: autism is often missed or mislabelled as anxiety, depression or a personality disorder.
  • Run by adult autism or neurodevelopmental services.

sections.heading: The tools assessors use
sections.html:
Tools give structure and consistency. They do not make the diagnosis. Services choose tools to suit the person's age, language and needs. The table below covers the ones you will see most in UK job adverts and reports.

ToolWhat it isUsed with
ADOS-2Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule. A semi-structured, play- or conversation-based observation lasting about 40 to 60 minutes, coded against set behaviours. Five modules chosen by age and spoken language (Toddler, then 1 to 4).12 months to adulthood
ADI-RAutism Diagnostic Interview, Revised. A long structured interview with a parent or carer about development and current behaviour. Often 1.5 to 3 hours.Mental age over 2; carer needed
DISCODiagnostic Interview for Social and Communication Disorders, developed by Lorna Wing and Judith Gould. A detailed interview that also maps wider needs and strengths. Training is run by the National Autistic Society.All ages
3diDevelopmental, Dimensional and Diagnostic Interview. A computer-assisted parent interview, shorter than the ADI-R.Children and young people
MIGDAS-2Monteiro Interview Guidelines for Diagnosing the Autism Spectrum. A sensory-based, conversational interview designed to feel more natural and to bring out the person's own perspective.Children, young people and adults
BOSABrief Observation of Symptoms of Autism. A shorter observation developed from the ADOS-2 for situations where a full ADOS-2 is not possible, for example with masks or remote assessment.Children and adults
ASDI and AAAInterview schedules for autistic people without a learning disability. Both are named in NICE CG142 for adults.Adults
SRS-2, SCQ, CARS-2Rating scales and questionnaires completed by parents, teachers or clinicians. Useful for gathering information across settings. Not diagnostic on their own.Mostly children
AQ, AQ-10, RAADS-R, CAT-QSelf-report questionnaires. The AQ-10 is a quick screen; RAADS-R is longer; CAT-Q measures camouflaging (masking). Screening only.Adults and older teens
Cognitive and sensory measuresFor example WISC-V or WAIS-IV (cognitive ability), and the Sensory Profile or Sensory Processing Measure. Used to build a profile and check for learning disability.Varies

Under NICE CG142, the formal tools suggested for adults without a learning disability are the AAA, ADI-R, ADOS, ASDI and RAADS-R; for adults with a learning disability, the ADOS and ADI-R. Children's guidance (CG128) does not name tools, but says to consider an autism-specific tool for the developmental history and for observation.

As an example of real-world practice, the private provider Compass Psychology describes using the ADI-R and ADOS-2 with at least two clinicians per assessment, plus cognitive testing where needed, and questionnaires such as the SCQ and SRS-2.

Most of these tools are "restricted": publishers sell them only to qualified professionals. For example, Hogrefe lists the ADOS-2 kit at qualification Level 3 and about £2,499 plus VAT for a hand-scored kit (November 2026).

sections.heading: How assessors are trained
sections.html:
Becoming an autism assessor is usually a specialism you add to a registered profession, not a job you train for from scratch. There are three layers.

1. A registered profession

ProfessionRegulatorTypical role in assessment
Clinical or counselling psychologistHCPCCan lead and diagnose; often runs ADOS-2, ADI-R and cognitive testing.
Educational psychologistHCPCContributes, especially for school-age children; may diagnose within some teams.
Psychiatrist or paediatricianGMCCan lead and diagnose; covers medical history, examination and co-occurring conditions.
Speech and language therapistHCPCAssesses communication and language; often co-runs the ADOS-2 within a team.
Occupational therapistHCPCAssesses sensory processing, motor skills and daily living within a team.
Nurse (learning disability or mental health)NMCAutism practitioner roles: history-taking, observation, coordination within a team.
Assistant psychologistNot regulatedSupports qualified staff: questionnaires, scoring, report drafting, under supervision.

The clinical psychology route is a psychology degree accredited by the British Psychological Society (BPS), relevant experience (often as an assistant psychologist), then a three-year, NHS-funded Doctorate in Clinical Psychology. Speech and language therapists and occupational therapists qualify through approved degree or master's courses; the Royal College of Speech and Language Therapists and the Royal College of Occupational Therapists list routes.

2. Tool training

The main tools need formal training before use. Courses in the UK as listed in November 2026 (prices change, so always check):

CourseProviderLengthApprox. price
Introduction to ADOS-2 (Modules 1 to 4)Hogrefe2 days online plus coding a video afterwards£600 + VAT
ADOS-2 Clinical TrainingPearson Clinical2 days online plus about 10 hours self-study (includes Toddler Module)£600 to £720
ADOS-2 trainingCompass Psychology4 days online plus coding a video afterwards£1,095 + VAT
ADI-R trainingCompass Psychology3 days online£895 + VAT
ADOS-2 and ADI-R Clinical ComboHogrefe5 days online£1,495 + VAT
DISCO trainingNational Autistic SocietySee providerSee provider

Things to know before you book:

  • Who can attend: providers expect a relevant degree and existing experience of autism. Hogrefe notes that some professions (for example educational psychologists, OTs, SLTs and nurses) can attend but would not make the final diagnostic decision on their own.
  • Clinical vs research reliability: clinical courses certify you for clinical use in the UK. Research reliability is a separate, stricter process, usually needing around 80% agreement with expert coding. Compass Psychology sells practice reliability videos.
  • Courses fill quickly: several Hogrefe dates for late 2026 and early 2027 were already fully booked when we checked.
  • A certificate is a start, not the finish. Pearson states plainly that attending the course is not enough to use the ADOS-2 competently.

3. Supervised practice

NHS England's operational guidance expects clinicians to use standardised tools only after training and enough experience, with sign-off as competent and ongoing supervision. In practice, new assessors co-run assessments with experienced colleagues, take part in team diagnostic discussions, and have their reports reviewed before working more independently. Useful extra learning includes autism in girls and women, masking, autism with learning disability, differential diagnosis, and neuro-affirming feedback and report writing.

sections.heading: How to get a job as an autism assessor
sections.html:
Where assessors work

  • NHS services: community paediatrics, CAMHS, adult autism or neurodevelopmental services, and learning disability teams. Salaried, with training and supervision built in.
  • Private and Right to Choose providers: in England, people referred for an assessment have a legal right to choose any provider that holds a relevant NHS contract, so many independent providers now carry out NHS-funded assessments (see an example NHS explanation and the Ombudsman's 2025 report). Roles are often sessional, part-time or remote.
  • Independent practice: experienced, registered clinicians run their own private assessment services. You will need your own insurance, tools, supervision and, depending on services offered, CQC registration.
  • Education and local authorities: educational psychology services contribute to assessments and to EHC needs assessments.

Typical NHS roles and pay

NHS roles are paid on Agenda for Change bands. Bands vary by trust and job, so treat these as a guide.

RoleTypical band2025/26 pay range (England)
Assistant psychologistBand 4 to 5£27,485 to £37,796
Autism practitioner (SLT, OT or nurse)Band 6 to 7£38,682 to £54,710
Clinical psychologist (newly qualified)Band 7£47,810 to £54,710
Senior or lead clinical psychologistBand 8a to 8b£55,690 to £74,896
Consultant psychologist or service leadBand 8c and abovefrom £76,965
Psychiatrists and paediatriciansMedical pay scalesSee NHS Employers

Pay ranges are the 2025/26 Agenda for Change rates published by NHS Employers, before any London or high-cost area supplement. They are approximate and may have changed since. Private providers often pay per assessment or per session; rates vary widely, so ask during recruitment.

Where jobs are advertised

  • NHS Jobs and Trac: search "autism assessment", "neurodevelopmental", "ASD pathway" or "ADOS".
  • BPS Appointments for psychology roles; RCSLT and RCOT job boards for therapists.
  • Careers pages of Right to Choose and private providers, and general boards such as LinkedIn and Indeed.
  • Word of mouth: many sessional roles are filled through ADOS-2 course contacts, supervision networks and professional groups.

A practical route in

  1. Get registered in a relevant profession (HCPC, GMC or NMC).
  2. Build autism experience in a team that assesses or supports autistic people, for example CAMHS, learning disability or a specialist school.
  3. Ask to shadow assessments and join diagnostic team meetings.
  4. Do ADOS-2 training, then ADI-R or another developmental interview. Many NHS teams will fund this once you are in post.
  5. Co-run assessments under supervision and keep a log of cases, ages and tools used.
  6. Apply for assessor roles, highlighting your tool training, supervised cases, report writing and understanding of NICE guidance and neuro-affirming practice.

label: Guide for professionals
title: Becoming an ADHD assessor in the UK
metaTitle: How to become an ADHD assessor in the UK: NHS and private practice | ND Resources
description: A UK guide for professionals on becoming an ADHD assessor: NICE NG87 assessment, the tools used (DIVA-5, ACE+, Conners 4, QbTest), training and prescribing, and NHS vs private practice jobs compared.
lede: How ADHD assessment works in the UK, the tools assessors use, how the skills are learnt, and how working in the NHS compares with private practice.
summary: ADHD is diagnosed by psychiatrists and paediatricians, and increasingly by trained specialist nurses and psychologists working in teams. Only prescribers can start medication.
Assessment follows NICE NG87: a full clinical interview, history from childhood, reports from others, and evidence of impairment in more than one setting. A questionnaire alone is never enough.
Common tools are the DIVA-5, ACE+, Conners 4, CAARS-2 and, for ages 6 to 17, QbTest.
NHS roles are salaried (about £38,700 to £62,700 for Band 6 to 8a in 2025/26); private and Right to Choose work is more flexible but brings extra rules on regulation and prescribing.

sections.heading: How ADHD assessment works in the UK
sections.html:
ADHD is diagnosed through a clinical assessment that looks at a person's attention, activity and impulsivity across their life and in different settings. In the UK, diagnosis follows NICE NG87 (Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: diagnosis and management), which covers children, young people and adults. Clinicians use the DSM-5-TR criteria for ADHD or the ICD-11 criteria (6A05).

Who can diagnose

NICE says a diagnosis should only be made by a specialist psychiatrist, a paediatrician, or another appropriately qualified healthcare professional with training and expertise in diagnosing ADHD. In practice that means:

  • Children: community paediatricians and child and adolescent psychiatrists, often with specialist ADHD nurses and psychologists in the team.
  • Adults: psychiatrists in adult ADHD or neurodevelopmental services, increasingly supported by specialist nurses, nurse prescribers, pharmacists and psychologists.
  • Psychologists often carry out the diagnostic assessment, especially in multidisciplinary and private services, but cannot prescribe. If medication is wanted, a prescriber reviews the case.

What a full assessment includes

  • A clinical interview about symptoms now and in childhood, often using a structured interview such as the DIVA-5 or ACE+.
  • Developmental and psychiatric history.
  • Reports from others: parents, partners, teachers or school reports, to show symptoms in more than one setting.
  • Impairment: NICE asks for symptoms that cause at least moderate psychological, social, educational or occupational impairment.
  • Mental state and physical health, including blood pressure, heart rate, weight and heart history if medication may follow.
  • Differential diagnosis and co-occurring conditions: anxiety, depression, trauma, sleep problems, bipolar disorder, substance use, learning difficulties and autism.
  • Feedback and a written report with recommendations for treatment, school or workplace adjustments.

As with autism, rating scales and questionnaires are aids, not answers. NICE is clear that ADHD should not be diagnosed from a rating scale or observation alone.

Why assessors are in demand

NHS England's independent ADHD Taskforce (final report November 2025) found that NHS services cannot currently meet demand. It reported waits of more than 2 years in many places, and 10 to 15 years in some areas. It recommended treating ADHD more like other common long-term conditions, sharing work between specialists, GPs and nurses, setting out what counts as an ADHD-qualified professional, and bringing all NHS and private ADHD providers under CQC oversight. Expect the rules on who can assess to become clearer and stricter over the next few years.

sections.heading: Children and adults: what differs
sections.html:
Children and young people

  • Referred by a GP, school, SENCO or health visitor.
  • Usually led by community paediatrics or CAMHS.
  • Parent and teacher rating scales (such as the Conners 4) are standard.
  • NICE recommends QbTest as an option for ages 6 to 17, alongside a full clinical assessment.
  • Parent training and school support come before or alongside medication for younger children.

Adults

  • Referred by a GP, often after a screening questionnaire such as the ASRS.
  • Led by adult ADHD or neurodevelopmental services, usually within mental health trusts.
  • Childhood history comes from the person, family and old school reports where available.
  • Many adults, especially women, were missed as children and have learned to compensate.
  • Medication is usually started by the specialist, then handed to the GP under a shared care agreement.

sections.heading: The tools assessors use
sections.html:
These are the tools most often named in UK reports and job adverts. Most are aids to a clinical interview, not tests that give a yes or no.

ToolWhat it isUsed with
DIVA-5Diagnostic Interview for ADHD in adults. A semi-structured interview based on DSM-5 that goes through each symptom in adulthood and childhood, with examples. Widely used in the NHS and private services. Downloaded per use (about €10 each, November 2026) from the DIVA Foundation. Young DIVA-5 covers ages 5 to 17 and DIVA-5 ID covers people with intellectual disability.Adults; versions for children
ACE and ACE+ADHD Child Evaluation (ACE) and its adult version (ACE+), semi-structured interviews developed by Professor Susan Young, freely available to clinicians.Children (ACE) and adults (ACE+)
ASRS v1.1Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale from the World Health Organization. Its 6-question Part A is a common GP screen.Adults
Conners 4 and CAARS-2Rating scales completed by the person, parents, teachers or a partner. Conners 4 covers ages 6 to 18; CAARS-2 covers adults. Sold to qualified professionals.Children and adults
SNAP-IV, VanderbiltShorter parent and teacher rating scales, often used for screening and monitoring.Children
QbTestA computer test that measures attention, impulsivity and movement. NICE recommends it as an option for ages 6 to 17, alongside a standard clinical assessment. For adults, NICE says it should be used only in research for now.6 to 17 (NHS use)
WFIRS, BRIEF-2Questionnaires on day-to-day impairment (WFIRS) and executive function (BRIEF-2).Children and adults
Cognitive testsFor example WISC-V or WAIS-IV, used where learning difficulties or a fuller profile need checking.Varies

For example, Compass Psychology describes using the DIVA-5 or Young DIVA-5, with at least two clinicians per assessment and optional cognitive testing.

sections.heading: How ADHD assessors are trained
sections.html:
1. A registered profession

ProfessionRegulatorCan diagnose?Can prescribe?
Psychiatrist (child or adult)GMCYesYes
PaediatricianGMCYes (children)Yes
GP with a special interestGMCIn some local schemes, with extra trainingUsually continues medication under shared care
Specialist ADHD nurseNMCIn many services, within a team and with trainingYes, if a qualified independent prescriber (V300)
Pharmacist prescriberGPhCNot usuallyYes, if an independent prescriber; mainly titration and reviews
Clinical or counselling psychologistHCPCYes in many services, within a teamNo
Occupational therapist or SLTHCPCContributes within a teamNo
Assistant psychologistNot regulatedNo; gathers information under supervisionNo

2. ADHD training

There is no single licence to assess ADHD. Employers look for recognised training, supervised practice and, for prescribers, an independent prescribing qualification. Courses listed in November 2026 (prices change, so always check):

CourseProviderLengthApprox. price
Adult ADHD Foundation CourseRoyal College of PsychiatristsAbout 10 hours online (e-learning plus a live day)£84 to £238 depending on membership
Adult ADHD diagnostic assessment and treatmentSouth London and Maudsley (Estia Centre)2 days online plus optional case discussions£1,078 (external)
Diagnosis and assessment of adults with ADHDUKAAN (via King's College London)See providerSee provider
DIVA-5 training videosDIVA FoundationOnline video seriesSee provider
Non-medical independent prescribing (V300)Universities approved by the NMC, GPhC or HCPCAbout 6 months part-timeOften funded by NHS employers
  • A certificate is not competence. The South London and Maudsley course says plainly that finishing it does not qualify anyone to practise independently as an ADHD assessor.
  • Know your limits: NICE expects people starting medication to have training and expertise in diagnosing and managing ADHD.
  • Watch for new standards: the ADHD Taskforce asked NHS England and the Department of Health and Social Care to define what an ADHD-qualified professional is.

3. Supervised practice

New assessors usually observe experienced colleagues, then run assessments with a senior clinician reviewing their reports and diagnostic decisions. Prescribers also learn titration, physical health monitoring and shared care before working independently.

sections.heading: NHS or private practice: jobs compared
sections.html:
Most ADHD assessors work in the NHS, in private practice, or both. This table sets out the main differences.

NHSPrivate practice and Right to Choose
Where you workCommunity paediatrics, CAMHS, adult ADHD or neurodevelopmental services in mental health trusts, and some GP-led local schemes.Private clinics, online providers, and independent providers holding NHS Right to Choose contracts. Some clinicians set up their own practice.
Who paysNHS-funded; free for patients.Patients pay privately, or the NHS pays through Right to Choose (England only).
EmploymentSalaried, Agenda for Change or medical pay scales, with pension, training and supervision.Employed, sessional or self-employed. Often paid per assessment or per session; rates vary, so ask.
Typical pay or fees2025/26 Agenda for Change: Band 6 £38,682 to £46,580; Band 7 £47,810 to £54,710; Band 8a £55,690 to £62,682.Fees to patients vary widely between providers. For example, Compass Psychology lists ADHD assessments from £1,895 (November 2026).
RegulationTrust governance, NHS clinical supervision and CQC-registered trusts.You must be registered (GMC, NMC, HCPC or GPhC), insured, and usually work for or register a CQC-registered service. Private prescribing of stimulants needs a private controlled drugs prescriber code and FP10PCD forms.
MedicationSpecialist starts and adjusts medication, then hands over to the GP under a shared care agreement.GPs can decline shared care with private providers, so patients may have to keep paying for prescriptions. Right to Choose providers usually follow NHS shared care rules.
ProsStable job, team support, training budgets, complex cases.Flexible hours, remote work, often higher earnings per assessment.
Watch out forLong waiting lists and heavy caseloads.Quality concerns in parts of the sector; the Taskforce wants all providers held to the same standards.

Typical NHS ADHD roles

RoleTypical band2025/26 pay range (England)
ADHD practitioner or assistant psychologistBand 4 to 5£27,485 to £37,796
Specialist ADHD nurseBand 6 to 7£38,682 to £54,710
ADHD nurse or pharmacist prescriber, clinical psychologistBand 7 to 8a£47,810 to £62,682
Lead nurse, senior psychologist or service leadBand 8a to 8c£55,690 to £88,682
Specialty doctor or consultant psychiatrist or paediatricianMedical pay scalesSee NHS Employers

Pay ranges are the 2025/26 Agenda for Change rates from NHS Employers, before London or high-cost area supplements. Bands vary by trust. Treat all figures as approximate and check current rates.

Where jobs are advertised

  • NHS Jobs and Trac: search "ADHD", "neurodevelopmental", "ADHD nurse" or "ADHD prescriber".
  • BPS Appointments, RCPsych and BMJ Careers for psychologists and doctors; nursing job boards for nurses.
  • Careers pages of private and Right to Choose providers, LinkedIn and Indeed.

A practical route in

  1. Get registered as a doctor, nurse, pharmacist or psychologist.
  2. Work in mental health, CAMHS or paediatrics to build experience with ADHD and the conditions it is often mixed up with.
  3. Shadow ADHD clinics and learn the DIVA-5 or ACE+ and the main rating scales.
  4. Take a recognised course, such as the RCPsych foundation course or an NHS trust programme.
  5. If you are a nurse or pharmacist, add independent prescribing (V300): prescribers are in particular demand.
  6. Assess under supervision and keep a log of cases, ages and outcomes.
  7. Then apply for NHS ADHD posts or sessional private work, or, once experienced, set up your own practice with the right insurance and CQC registration.

label: Guide for professionals
title: Becoming a non-medical prescriber in the UK
metaTitle: How to become a non-medical prescriber (V300) in the UK | ND Resources
description: A UK guide to becoming a non-medical (independent) prescriber: who can train, NHS-funded vs self-funded routes, V300 courses at 32 universities compared, finding a DPP or practice assessor, and a free checklist PDF.
lede: Who can train as a prescriber, NHS-funded and self-funded routes compared, V300 courses at 32 UK universities side by side, ideas for finding a prescribing assessor, and a free step-by-step checklist.
summary: Nurses, midwives, pharmacists, and some allied health professionals (such as physiotherapists, paramedics and podiatrists) can train as independent prescribers after at least a year of registered practice.
The course usually takes about 6 months part-time, with taught days, about 90 hours of supervised practice and exams.
NHS-funded places come through your employer's prescribing lead or training hub. Self-funded fees listed by universities range from about £1,400 to £3,200 (November 2026).
You need a Designated Prescribing Practitioner (DPP) or practice assessor, an experienced prescriber who signs off your competence.

sections.heading: What a non-medical prescriber is, and who can train
sections.html:
A non-medical prescriber is a registered healthcare professional, who is not a doctor or dentist, and is legally allowed to prescribe after completing an approved prescribing programme. Most people now train as independent prescribers, which means they can assess, diagnose and prescribe within their own competence. Nurses take a course called the V300.

ProfessionRegulatorType of prescribing
Nurses and midwivesNMCIndependent and supplementary (V300). Community nurses may do the more limited V100 or V150.
PharmacistsGPhCIndependent. Pharmacists qualifying from 2026 register as prescribers straight away.
Physiotherapists, podiatrists, therapeutic radiographersHCPCIndependent and supplementary
ParamedicsHCPCIndependent and supplementary, usually in advanced practice roles
Dietitians and diagnostic radiographersHCPCSupplementary only (prescribing within an agreed plan with a doctor)
OptometristsGOCIndependent, for eye conditions

Non-medical prescribers are a big part of the ADHD and mental health workforce: specialist nurses and pharmacists often adjust ADHD medication and review patients. See our ADHD assessor guide.

sections.heading: How the training works
sections.html:
All courses are approved by the regulators and follow the same core design: taught days, supervised learning in practice, and exams.

  • Length: usually about 6 months part-time.
  • Level: Level 6 (degree) or Level 7 (master's), usually 30 to 45 credits.
  • Taught days: often about 26 days, in person or online.
  • Learning in practice: commonly about 90 hours (12 days) with your prescribing supervisor.
  • Assessment: a pharmacology exam, a numeracy test (usually 100% needed), a portfolio of practice, and sign-off by your assessor.
  • Standards: the Competency Framework for all Prescribers and, for nurses, the NMC standards for prescribing programmes.

Not sure what to read? See our recommended books for prescribers, from V300 course texts to the BNF.

sections.heading: NHS-funded or self-funded: routes compared
sections.html:
You can train with your employer's support and NHS funding, or pay for the course yourself. Both lead to exactly the same qualification.

NHS-fundedSelf-funded or privately funded
Who can applyStaff in NHS trusts, GP practices and some NHS-contracted services.Anyone eligible, including people in private clinics, agencies and self-employment.
Who pays the feeNHS England (regional workforce teams) or your employer. Primary care places often go through local training hubs.You, or your private employer.
Course feeUsually nothing to you.About £1,400 to £3,200 listed in November 2026; most are £1,700 to £2,600. See the table below.
How to applyThrough your trust or practice Non-Medical Prescribing lead, who often has limited places and set deadlines.Directly to the university, often still needing a sign-off from the clinical setting where you will learn.
Study timeProtected study days are often agreed with your employer.You may need to use annual leave or unpaid time.
Finding a DPPUsually arranged inside your team or practice.You need to find your own DPP or practice assessor, and a setting that will host your supervised hours.
After qualifyingYou prescribe under your employer's policies, and your role may be re-banded.You need your own indemnity cover, governance and, for some medicines, a private prescriber code.
Watch out forSome funding comes with a commitment to stay with your employer for a set time.Universities may turn down self-funded applicants who do not have a suitable clinical role or DPP.

sections.heading: Finding your prescribing assessor (DPP)
sections.html:
Every trainee needs an experienced prescriber to supervise and sign them off. The names vary by regulator:

  • Designated Prescribing Practitioner (DPP): the term used by the GPhC and HCPC, and now widely by universities for all professions.
  • Practice assessor and practice supervisor: the NMC terms for nurses and midwives. The assessor signs off your competence; the supervisor supports you day to day.

Since the Royal College of Pharmacy (formerly the Royal Pharmaceutical Society) published its DPP competency framework, your DPP does not have to be a doctor. They can be any experienced prescriber, for example a GP, a consultant, or an experienced nurse or pharmacist prescriber. Universities usually expect:

  • active prescribing for at least 3 years (some universities ask for less);
  • experience in the same area you will prescribe in;
  • meeting the DPP competencies, often shown through a self-assessment;
  • time to supervise you and to assess you fairly.

Ideas for finding a DPP or practice assessor

  • Start with your own workplace. A consultant, GP, advanced practitioner or senior nurse or pharmacist prescriber you already work with is the easiest option, because they know your practice.
  • Ask your Non-Medical Prescribing lead. Most NHS trusts, ICBs and larger GP groups have one, and many keep a list of prescribers willing to supervise.
  • Contact your local primary care training hub. Training hubs support GP practice staff and can often link trainees with practices that host prescribing students.
  • Look for GP training practices. Practices approved to train GP registrars are used to supervising learners. Your regional NHS England workforce, training and education team lists them.
  • Ask the university. Course teams cannot always find a DPP for you, but they can confirm who is eligible and sometimes know local prescribers who help.
  • Choose someone in your future scope. If you want to prescribe for ADHD, approach a psychiatrist or experienced ADHD nurse prescriber in an ADHD clinic, including Right to Choose or private providers you work with.
  • Use professional networks. Specialist nurse and pharmacist networks, professional body forums, LinkedIn groups and contacts from earlier courses or placements.
  • Think about former colleagues and mentors who now prescribe, as long as they can supervise you in a real clinical setting.
  • Paid supervision: some experienced prescribers offer DPP supervision for a fee, mainly to self-funded students. Check first that your university accepts this, and agree in writing what is included.

How to ask

  • Send a short, polite email: your profession, the course and dates, the area you will prescribe in, and what is needed (usually about 90 hours of supervised practice and a final sign-off).
  • Attach the university's DPP or practice assessor guidance so they can check they are eligible.
  • Offer flexibility: supervised hours can often be spread across clinics over several months.
  • Agree early how often you will meet and how they will assess you, and put it in your learning agreement.

ND Resources does not recommend individual supervisors. Your university must approve your DPP or practice assessor.

sections.heading: Step-by-step checklist
sections.html:
Use this checklist to plan each stage. You can also download it as a free PDF to print or fill in. No sign-up is needed.

1. Before you apply

  • Check your profession can prescribe independently (see the professions table in the guide) and that you are on the NMC, HCPC or GPhC register.
  • Have at least 1 year of post-registration experience in the area you will prescribe in (check your course: some ask for more).
  • Check you have the academic level the course needs (usually Level 6 study for a Level 6 course; a degree or 120 Level 6 credits for Level 7).
  • Decide your scope of practice: the conditions and medicines you will prescribe for, for example ADHD or mental health.
  • Get written support from your line manager or, if self-employed, a clinical setting that will host your learning.
  • Have an enhanced DBS check from the last 3 years, or the DBS update service.

2. Find your supervisors

  • Find a Designated Prescribing Practitioner (DPP) or practice assessor: an experienced prescriber, usually with at least 3 years of prescribing, who meets the DPP competency framework.
  • Find a practice supervisor (NMC courses), who can be the same or a different person.
  • Complete the DPP competency self-assessment together and agree how you will meet the required supervised hours.
  • Arrange the placement or learning-environment audit your university asks for.

3. Funding and application

  • NHS route: ask your trust or practice Non-Medical Prescribing lead, or your local primary care training hub, about a funded place.
  • Self-funded route: compare course fees, start dates and attendance, and budget for fees plus time off work.
  • Get your NMP lead or employer to approve the application, then apply to the university by its deadline.

4. During the course

  • Attend taught days and pass the pharmacology and numeracy exams (numeracy usually needs 100%).
  • Complete your supervised practice hours (often about 90 hours) and keep a log.
  • Build your portfolio against the Competency Framework for all Prescribers.
  • Get your DPP or practice assessor to sign off your competence at the end.

5. After you qualify

  • Your university tells your regulator, and your prescribing qualification is added to the register. Check it appears before you prescribe.
  • Register as a prescriber with your employer and follow its prescribing policy.
  • Write down your scope of practice and keep within it.
  • For private work, get indemnity cover that includes prescribing; for controlled drugs, apply for a private prescriber code if needed.
  • Keep up CPD and audit your prescribing each year.

title: Assessment tools
metaTitle: Assessment tools: autism assessment methods explained | ND Resources
description: Articles for UK professionals on how autism and neurodevelopmental assessments for children are carried out, starting with ADOS-2 compared with online observations.
lede: Articles for professionals on how neurodevelopmental assessments for children are carried out, the tools used, and how in-person and online methods compare.
checkedNote: New articles are added over time.

sections.heading: About this section
sections.html:
Assessing a child for autism or another neurodevelopmental condition brings together several kinds of information: what parents and teachers have noticed, the child's developmental history, and time spent observing and playing with the child. These articles explain the main methods used in the UK in plain language, compare them, and point to the evidence.

They are written for clinicians, students, SENCOs and anyone who works alongside assessment teams. They are not a substitute for formal training in any assessment tool.

Related guides: Becoming an autism assessor in the UK and Becoming an ADHD assessor in the UK.

label: Section for professionals
title: Screening tools
metaTitle: Free screening tools for autism and ADHD | ND Resources
description: Where UK professionals can download autism and ADHD screening tools from their official sources, plus the Coventry Grid, with notes on how to use them well.
lede: Autism and ADHD screening tools in one place, with links to each official download and notes on using them well.
checkedNote: Links and terms checked on this date. Tools are linked to their official source, not copied here.
summary: A screening tool tells you whether a full assessment is worth doing. It never gives a diagnosis, and a low score never rules a condition out.
We link to each tool’s official source instead of hosting copies, because most tools are copyrighted and their authors update them.
Screen for more than one thing: autism, ADHD, anxiety, OCD and trauma often overlap or look alike.
Women and others who mask are often missed by screening questionnaires, so give weight to their history and own account.

sections.heading: Using screening tools well
sections.html:
• Screen, then assess. A score above the cut-off means a full assessment may be needed. A score below it does not mean the person is not autistic or does not have ADHD, especially if their history suggests otherwise.
  • Use the right version. Check age, language and learning disability. NICE suggests the AQ-10 only for adults without a moderate or severe learning disability.
  • Look wider. Repetitive behaviour, inattention and social difficulty can come from autism, ADHD, anxiety, OCD or trauma. Ask about all of them. For OCD, see OCD and neurodivergence.
  • Use the official copy. Download from the source linked below, keep the credit line, and do not change the wording.
  • Explain the result. Tell the person what the score means, and what it does not mean.

sections.heading: Autism
sections.html:

sections.heading: Coventry Grid: autism, attachment and trauma
sections.html:
Children who have had early trauma or disrupted care can show social difficulties, rigid behaviour and sensory needs that look like autism. The Coventry Grid, developed by clinical psychologist Heather Moran (first published in 2010, Version 2 in 2015), sets out side by side how these needs tend to differ across areas such as social interaction, play, routines and sensory responses.

It is very useful for structuring observation and history-taking, but it is not a diagnostic tool and has no cut-off scores. A 2022 review (Davidson, Moran and Minnis) notes that it came from clinical experience and that the research on it is still limited. A child can be autistic and also have attachment or trauma needs.

sections.heading: Women and late diagnosis
sections.html:
Many autistic women are diagnosed late, often in midlife, after years of being misunderstood or misdiagnosed. In Leedham et al. (2020), eleven women diagnosed after the age of 40 described autism as a hidden condition. Diagnosis helped them make sense of their past and move from being self-critical to being kinder to themselves, although it took time to accept and others did not always respond well.

What this means for screening:

  • People who mask (camouflage) their differences can score low on screening questionnaires. Give weight to their history and their own account.
  • Ask about effort and exhaustion, not just what others can see.
  • The CAT-Q (Camouflaging Autistic Traits Questionnaire, 25 items) can open a conversation about masking. Its authors say it is not a screening or diagnostic tool and has no cut-off score, so do not use it to decide on referral or diagnosis.
  • Offer support after diagnosis. The women in the study described needing time and help to adjust.

label: Guide for professionals
title: OCD and neurodivergence
metaTitle: OCD with autism and ADHD: co-occurrence and differential diagnosis | ND Resources
description: A UK guide for professionals on OCD in autistic people and people with ADHD: how often they co-occur, how to tell them apart, screening tools and adapting treatment.
lede: How OCD co-occurs with autism and ADHD, how to tell them apart, which screening tools to use, and how to adapt treatment.
summary: OCD is more common in autistic people and in people with ADHD than in the general population, and the conditions can look alike.
In children and young people, a 2024 meta-analysis found OCD in about 1 in 9 autistic young people, and autism in about 1 in 10 young people with OCD.
The key question for autism is how the behaviour feels: autistic routines are usually wanted and calming, OCD compulsions are usually unwanted and driven by fear.
OCD can look like ADHD, because intrusive thoughts and rituals use up attention. Consider both, and treat both when both are present.

sections.heading: What OCD is
sections.html:
Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) involves obsessions (unwanted, distressing thoughts, images or urges) and compulsions (things a person feels they must do, physically or in their head, to ease that distress or prevent harm). It is usually diagnosed when it takes up more than an hour a day or causes clear distress or problems in daily life.

OCD is not a personality trait or a liking for tidiness. Common themes include contamination, harm, checking, symmetry and “just right” feelings, and unwanted taboo thoughts. Many people hide their rituals, so ask directly.

sections.heading: OCD and autism
sections.html:
OCD and autism often occur together. A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of children and young people (Aymerich et al.) found OCD in about 11.6% of autistic young people and autism in about 9.5% of young people with OCD. Young people with both had more difficulties overall and responded less well to standard CBT.

Autistic repetitive behaviour is usually ego-syntonic: it fits with what the person wants. OCD compulsions are usually ego-dystonic: the person experiences them as unwanted. This can be hard to judge in young children and in people who find it hard to describe their inner experience, so gather information from several sources over time.

Question to exploreMore like autismMore like OCD
How does it feel?Calming, enjoyable or comforting. The person usually wants to keep doing it.Unwanted and distressing. The person often wishes they could stop.
What drives it?Predictability, sensory need, interest or regulation.Fear, doubt or a feeling that something bad will happen, or a sense of things not being “just right”.
Is there an obsession behind it?Usually no feared thought; the behaviour is the point.Usually yes: an intrusive thought, image or urge comes first.
When did it start?Present since early childhood, part of how the person has always been.Often starts or changes later, sometimes quite suddenly.
What happens if it is stopped?Distress from change or loss of routine.Rising anxiety about the feared outcome, with brief relief once the ritual is done.
ContentSpecial interests, sameness, lining up or ordering for its own sake.Contamination, harm, checking, symmetry, unwanted taboo thoughts, reassurance seeking.

DSM-5 says OCD should not be diagnosed when repetitive behaviour is better explained by autism, but a person can have both. Watch for change: rituals that grow, become more distressing or start to take over are a reason to assess for OCD.

sections.heading: OCD and ADHD
sections.html:
OCD and ADHD also co-occur, although reported rates vary widely between studies because of how they were done. A 2019 review (Cabarkapa et al.) reported co-occurring ADHD in about 11.8% of people with OCD, and higher estimates in children. A 2015 review (Abramovitch et al.) warned that ADHD-like symptoms caused by OCD may be misdiagnosed as ADHD.

What you seeCan come from ADHDCan come from OCD
Poor concentrationAttention drifts to whatever is most interesting.Attention is pulled inward by intrusive thoughts or mental rituals.
Slow to finish tasksDistraction, starting late, losing track of time.Checking, repeating or redoing until it feels right.
Forgetting or losing thingsWorking memory and organisation difficulties.Doubt about memory, leading to repeated checking.
Acting without thinkingImpulsivity: acting quickly, then regretting it.Compulsions are deliberate and planned to prevent harm, not impulsive.
RestlessnessPhysical restlessness and need to move.Restlessness from anxiety, or tics if there is also a tic disorder.

Ask what is going on in the person’s head when they lose focus. Someone with OCD can often describe a specific worry or ritual; someone with ADHD more often describes drifting to something else. Consider undiagnosed ADHD when OCD does not respond to treatment, and the other way round.

sections.heading: Tics and Tourette’s
sections.html: OCD, ADHD and tic disorders often run together. Some repetitive movements are tics (sudden, quick and hard to hold back), and some are compulsions (done to ease a fear or a “not right” feeling). Ask what the person feels just before the movement.

sections.heading: Screening tools for OCD
sections.html:
NICE CG31 says professionals should routinely consider OCD in people at higher risk, such as those with depression, anxiety, alcohol or drug misuse, body dysmorphic disorder or an eating disorder. A positive screen means a full assessment, not a diagnosis. More tools are on the Screening tools page.

sections.heading: Treatment and adjustments
sections.html:
• Talking therapy. NICE CG31 recommends cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention (ERP). For autistic people, it often works better with clear structure, literal language, visual supports, more time and family involvement.
  • Separate autism from OCD in the plan. Do not target autistic routines and interests that the person values. Focus ERP on the behaviours driven by fear.
  • Medication. SSRIs are used for OCD. For people with ADHD, some reports suggest stimulants can worsen OCD symptoms, although the evidence is limited. Start or change one medicine at a time so that effects are clear, and monitor both conditions.
  • Treat both. Untreated ADHD can reduce the benefit of OCD treatment. Treating both together is linked to better outcomes.

label: Assessment tools
title: ADOS-2 vs Online Observations
metaTitle: ADOS-2 vs Online Observations in autism assessment for children | ND Resources
description: How in-person ADOS-2 and online observations are carried out in autism assessments for children, teenagers and adults (Modules 3 and 4), how the activities compare, and what the evidence says.
lede: How in-person ADOS-2 and online observations are carried out with children, teenagers and adults, how the activities compare, and what the research says.
checkedNote: Research on remote assessment is still developing.
summary: The ADOS-2 is a standardised, in-person observation using a set kit and one of five modules chosen by the child's age and language. It takes about 40 to 60 minutes and is scored with an algorithm.
Online observations adapt the same ideas for video. Usually a parent leads play at home while the clinician coaches and observes. It is not standardised and has no validated scores.
Modules 3 and 4 are for fluent speakers, including teenagers and adults (Module 4). Because they rely more on conversation, they adapt more easily to online observation.
Studies find telehealth and in-person assessments agree in about 80 to 88% of children, but the evidence has weaknesses.
Neither method diagnoses on its own. Many services now use a hybrid model.

sections.heading: In-person ADOS-2
sections.html:
The ADOS-2 (Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule, Second Edition) is a standardised, semi-structured observation. A trained clinician spends time with the child using a set of planned activities and materials. The activities are designed to create natural opportunities for the child to communicate, share interest, play and use their imagination, so the clinician can observe how the child responds and starts interactions.

How it is carried out

  • Who: a clinician trained in the ADOS-2, often with a second clinician observing or co-coding. Many UK teams video-record sessions, with consent, for later review.
  • Where: a quiet clinic room, set up with the standard ADOS-2 kit of toys and materials.
  • How long: usually about 40 to 60 minutes.
  • Which version: the clinician chooses one of five modules based on the child's age and spoken language, from a Toddler Module for children from about 12 months who are not yet using phrases, to modules for children using single words, phrases, or fluent speech.
  • Afterwards: the clinician codes what they saw against set behaviour areas. A scoring algorithm gives a classification and a comparison score that shows how many autism-related features were observed.
  • What it is not: a test that diagnoses on its own. NICE is clear that no single tool should be relied on to diagnose autism. The ADOS-2 is one source of information alongside the developmental history, reports from home and school, and clinical judgement.

The ADOS-2 is published by Western Psychological Services and sold in the UK by Hogrefe to qualified professionals only. This article describes it in general terms and does not reproduce any of its activities, codes or scoring.

sections.heading: Online observations
sections.html:
During the COVID-19 pandemic, many UK services began assessing children over video. Because the ADOS-2 is standardised for face-to-face use with its own materials, it is not validated for remote use and should not be scored over video. Instead, clinicians carry out online observations: they borrow its ideas about which situations reveal social communication differences, but adapt them for a screen and a home setting. Reports should describe these as online observations, not as ADOS-2 results.

How it is carried out

  • Who leads the play: usually the parent or carer, with the clinician coaching them through each activity over video. With older, verbal children, the clinician may talk with the child directly on screen.
  • Where: the child's home, using the family's own toys or a small set of everyday items the service asks them to gather or sends in advance.
  • How long: the observed activities are often short, around 15 to 30 minutes, within a longer video appointment.
  • Set-up: a laptop or tablet placed so the clinician can see the child's face and hands, a quiet space, and a stable internet connection. Some services do a short technology check first.
  • Afterwards: clinicians describe what they observed and use clinical judgement. There is no validated algorithm or cut-off score for most remote approaches.

Named remote tools

  • BOSA (Brief Observation of Symptoms of Autism): developed by the ADOS-2 authors in 2020. A parent or carer leads a short set of play and conversation activities, about 12 to 14 minutes, while a trained clinician watches in person, through a one-way mirror or by video. There are versions for minimally verbal children, phrase speech, and fluent speech at different ages. Dow and colleagues, 2021.
  • TELE-ASD-PEDS: a caregiver-led set of about eight short play activities, around 15 to 20 minutes, designed for children under 3, developed at Vanderbilt University in the United States.
  • Service-designed protocols: many NHS and private teams have written their own online observation schedules. Quality and consistency vary between services.

sections.heading: Teenagers and adults: Modules 3 and 4
sections.html:
The ADOS-2 is not only for young children. Its two fluent-speech modules are also used with teenagers and adults, and online observations are now common in adult autism services.

ModuleWho it is forWhat it focuses on
Module 3Children and younger teenagers who speak fluentlyA mix of play-based and conversation-based activities, suited to children who still enjoy toys and pretend play.
Module 4Older teenagers and adults who speak fluentlyMainly conversation: everyday life, work or study, friendships, relationships and emotions, with fewer toy-based activities.

Online observations with teenagers and adults

  • Conversation adapts well to video. Because Modules 3 and 4 rely more on talking than on toys, many of their activity types can be carried out with the clinician speaking directly to the young person or adult on screen, without a parent leading.
  • Some things are harder online: eye contact, gestures, body language and the natural back-and-forth of conversation can look different on a video call, for autistic and non-autistic people alike.
  • Masking: many teenagers and adults, especially girls and women, have learned to hide autistic traits. Being at home may help some people relax, but a short observation in either setting can still miss masked traits, so history and self-report matter even more.
  • UK evidence: an adult autism diagnostic service study (BJPsych Open, 2023) compared 163 adults observed online with 198 observed in person before the pandemic. It found no significant difference in total observation scores between the two groups, and most patients and clinicians were positive about the online option. The authors note their clinic sees many people with additional mental health difficulties, so results may not apply everywhere.

As with children, online observations with adults are not the standardised ADOS-2 and should be reported as observations, used alongside a full clinical interview and developmental history.

sections.heading: Activities compared
sections.html:
This table compares the general types of activity used, not the actual ADOS-2 tasks, which are protected by copyright and only available to trained users.

Type of activityIn-person ADOS-2Online observation
Free play with toysClinician offers a standard set of toys and watches how the child explores and plays.Child plays with their own toys at home; parent joins in as coached. More natural, but toys and set-up differ for each child.
Sharing attention and interestClinician creates moments to see whether the child follows a point or shows things to others.Parent tries similar moments, guided by the clinician. Harder to see eye gaze and pointing clearly on camera.
Responding to name and social bidsClinician and parent call the child in a planned way.Parent does this at home. Easy to adapt, but sound and camera angle can hide responses.
Requests and turn-taking gamesClinician sets up simple games and routines with the kit.Parent plays familiar games such as bubbles or peekaboo. The child may be more relaxed, but games are less standard.
Pretend and imaginative playClinician uses standard figures and objects to invite pretend play.Uses the child's own toys. Familiar toys can lead to well-practised routines that look more flexible than they are.
Conversation (verbal children)Face-to-face conversation about the child's life, interests, feelings and relationships.Conversation over video. Works for many older children, but video calls change the natural flow of turn-taking and eye contact.
Describing pictures or a storyClinician uses standard picture and story materials.Clinician shares a picture or book on screen. Possible, but screen size and attention can affect performance.
Sensory interests and repetitive behavioursObserved throughout in an unfamiliar clinic room.Observed at home, where the child may be more comfortable and show everyday behaviours, or may be distracted by familiar things.
Who interacts with the childTrained clinician.Mostly parent or carer, coached by the clinician.
ScoringStandard coding and algorithm, with a classification and comparison score.Descriptive. No validated scores for most approaches; the BOSA has standard coding but no established cut-offs yet.
TimeAbout 40 to 60 minutes.Often 15 to 30 minutes of observed activities.

sections.heading: Strengths and limitations
sections.html:
In-person ADOS-2

Strengths

  • Standardised, with decades of research and known accuracy.
  • Same materials and situations for every child, so results can be compared.
  • The clinician interacts directly and can adjust their approach in the moment.
  • Easier to see eye contact, gestures and subtle social cues.

Limitations

  • An unfamiliar clinic can make some children anxious or shut down.
  • Travel and waiting rooms can be hard for families.
  • Needs expensive kits, trained staff and suitable rooms.
  • Shows one short window of behaviour in one setting.

Online observation

Strengths

  • Child is seen at home, where they may be more relaxed.
  • No travel, fewer missed appointments, and easier to fit around families.
  • Clinicians can see how the child interacts with a parent, which a clinic observation does not show.
  • Useful for some children with selective mutism or high anxiety about new places.

Limitations

  • Not standardised, so findings are less comparable between children and services.
  • Camera angles and connection problems can hide or distort social cues.
  • Depends on the parent's confidence in leading the activities.
  • Needs a device, internet and a quiet space, which not every family has.
  • Safeguarding and risk are harder to manage remotely.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
sections.html:
• Agreement is fairly good overall. A 2023 systematic review of 18 studies and 1,593 children found that telehealth and in-person assessments reached the same diagnostic decision in about 80 to 88% of cases. However, many of the studies had weaknesses in their design.
  • UK clinicians are cautiously positive. An NHS England-funded study of 45 clinicians (Spain and colleagues, 2022) found most wanted to keep telehealth as part of a hybrid model, but worried about consistency, judging social cues on screen, digital poverty and the untested nature of adapted ADOS-2 approaches.
  • The BOSA is useful but not a replacement. In a UK NHS community paediatric service, 92% of ADOS-2-trained clinicians found the full ADOS-2 more helpful for diagnosis than the BOSA (Shapter and colleagues, 2024). They valued seeing parent and child together, but felt the BOSA gave less information about imagination and relationships.
  • National guidance. NICE guidance on children's autism assessment (CG128) does not cover telehealth. NHS England's national assessment framework says remote assessments need extra safeguards and should be offered with in-person options.

When each approach may suit

SituationUsually better
Very young or minimally verbal childrenIn person
Complex picture or several possible diagnosesIn person
Online observation was unclear or inconclusiveIn person, as a follow-up
Safeguarding concernsIn person
Severe anxiety about clinics or selective mutismOnline, or hybrid
Long travel distances or a family that cannot easily attendOnline, or hybrid
Seeing the child in their everyday setting would add useful informationOnline, alongside in-person
Early triage or a first look before deciding on next stepsOnline

Many UK services now use a hybrid model: history-taking and parent interviews by video, with an in-person observation when needed. Whatever the method, the diagnosis should rest on all the information together and on clinical judgement.
